sections.title: Very short answer questions. Answer in 30–50 words.

questions.q: What do you mean by political democracy and social democracy?
questions.answer: Political democracy has political conditions — a Constitution vesting power in the people, fundamental rights, universal adult franchise, a responsible government and free press. Social democracy means equality of social status and opportunity, social welfare and economic development reaching everyone, especially the poor.

questions.q: Explain any two essential conditions for democracy.
questions.answer: (1) A Constitution that vests supreme power in the people and protects rights, with universal adult franchise and regular free elections. (2) Social and economic equality — education for all, social security and the fruits of development reaching the poor; also a responsible government and a free press.

questions.q: How does illiteracy affect the working of democracy?
questions.answer: Illiterate citizens may not understand issues, rights and policies, so they cannot vote meaningfully or ensure that representatives truly represent their interests; they are easily misled. Literacy makes people aware of liberty and equality and helps them participate actively.

questions.q: Why is poverty called the greatest bane of democracy?
questions.answer: A hungry person cares first for food, so the right to vote means little to him. Poverty denies people opportunities for a healthy, fulfilling life, keeps them unequal and dependent, and they can be bribed or exploited during elections.

sections.title: Short answer questions. Answer in 50–80 words.

questions.q: Suggest any three ways to strengthen Indian democracy.
questions.answer: (1) Achieve universal literacy and reduce poverty and inequality so that every citizen can participate meaningfully. (2) Check corruption, criminalisation of politics and the use of caste and religion in elections through electoral, administrative and judicial reforms. (3) Citizens must vote wisely, use the RTI Act and peaceful protest to keep representatives accountable, and respect others' rights and views.

or.q: Suggest any three ways to empower women.
or.answer: (1) Education and skills for girls, with equal access to health care and jobs and equal pay. (2) Political empowerment through reservation in panchayats, municipalities and legislatures. (3) Strict enforcement of laws against foeticide, dowry and violence, and changing attitudes so that girls and boys are treated equally (National Policy for Empowerment of Women, 2001).

questions.q: How is casteism a challenge to Indian democracy? Explain in three points.
questions.answer: (1) Untouchability and caste discrimination persist despite the constitutional ban, denying Dalits dignity and opportunities. (2) Politicisation of caste and 'casteisation of politics' — parties use caste as vote-banks for narrow gains, weakening issues-based politics. (3) It keeps socio-economic inequalities alive and sometimes causes caste violence, against the democratic ideals of equality and fraternity.

or.q: How is criminalisation of politics a challenge to Indian democracy? Explain in three points.
or.answer: (1) People with criminal records contest and win elections using money and muscle power, negating democratic values. (2) Violence and intimidation stop voters from voting freely and spoil free and fair elections. (3) Criminals in power protect lawbreakers, increase corruption and reduce public trust; courts and alert voters must reject such candidates.

questions.q: Suggest any three corrective measures for universal literacy (education for all).
questions.answer: (1) Free and compulsory education for all children of 6–14 years under the RTE Act 2009 and Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan. (2) Adult literacy through the National Literacy Mission and Saakshar Bharat (functional literacy for those above 15). (3) Special attention to girls and disadvantaged groups — scholarships, mid-day meals, more schools in remote areas.

questions.q: Explain any three tools available to a common citizen for making the government accountable.
questions.answer: (1) The vote — citizens can remove a government that does not perform. (2) The Right to Information Act 2005 — to ask for information on government decisions and spending. (3) The media, petitions, civil society organisations and peaceful protest, satyagraha or civil disobedience to point out failures and demand action.

questions.q: 'Discrimination against girls and women exists in every walk of life.' Support the statement.
questions.answer: (1) The declining sex ratio (940 in 2011) and child sex ratio (914) show son preference, female foeticide and neglect of girls. (2) Female literacy (65.46%) is far below male literacy (82.14%), and girls do more household work while boys go to school. (3) Women get fewer jobs, lower pay and little representation in Parliament and public life; maternal mortality is high.

questions.q: How does literacy play an important role in the success of a democracy?
questions.answer: (1) Literate citizens understand issues, policies and candidates and vote wisely. (2) They know their rights and duties and principles of liberty and equality, so they can make representatives accountable. (3) They take part in public life, resist exploitation and support development; that is why universal literacy is a must for democracy.

sections.title: Long answer questions. Answer in 80–120 words.

questions.q: What are the major challenges faced by Indian democracy? Explain any six.
questions.answer: (1) Illiteracy — many cannot fully understand issues and rights. (2) Poverty and unemployment — the greatest bane of democracy. (3) Gender discrimination — low sex ratio, female literacy and representation. (4) Casteism, communalism and religious fundamentalism — vote-banks, riots and inequality. (5) Regionalism arising from regional imbalances, sometimes leading to separatism. (6) Corruption, criminalisation of politics and political violence, which undermine free elections and trust in institutions.

questions.q: What corrective measures are needed to meet the challenges to Indian democracy?
questions.answer: (1) Universal literacy — RTE Act, Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan, Saakshar Bharat. (2) Poverty alleviation — self-employment (SGSY, self-help groups) and wage employment (MGNREGA). (3) Elimination of gender discrimination — 73rd/74th Amendments, National Policy for Empowerment of Women 2001. (4) Removal of regional imbalance — Tribal, Hill, Border, Desert and Drought-Prone Area programmes. (5) Administrative and judicial reforms — accountable, transparent, e-governance; faster justice and more judges. (6) Sustainable development and an active role of citizens in participation and accountability.
